conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how things have been feeling for you since your baby arrived. We’ll use a short, well-studied questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale** (the EPDS). It’s simply ten questions that help us see whether you might be experiencing postpartum depression or anxiety, and it includes one question about self-harm so we can keep you safe.  

Everything you share is confidential, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you in the past seven days. We’ll go through one question at a time; if you need a break or want to skip anything, just let me know. Ready to start?

1. Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

(soft sigh)  
I’ve laughed a little—like when my partner made a silly face at the baby—but most of the time it feels kind of forced. Things that used to seem really funny just don’t grab me the same way anymore.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really… I marked the one that says “not quite so much now.” I can still chuckle here and there, but it feels kind of flat, like I’m pretending more than actually feeling it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I picked “rather less than I used to.” I still try to plan small things—like taking the baby for a short walk or having coffee with a friend—but the excitement isn’t really there. Mostly it feels like another task on my list instead of something I truly look forward to.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

I chose “yes, some of the time.” When the baby won’t settle or I can’t get her to nap, I keep thinking it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m not patient enough or I missed some cue. My head tells me it’s normal newborn stuff, but the guilty feeling still creeps in.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

I picked “yes, very often.” I know some worry is normal, but even when everything looks fine—she’s breathing fine, no fever—I still lie awake running through all the “what-ifs.” It’s like my mind jumps to the worst possibility before I can stop it.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

I marked “yes, quite a lot.” It hits suddenly—my heart races and I feel shaky, like something awful is about to happen, even if the baby’s asleep and the house is quiet. I’ll check her breathing over and over, but the scared feeling doesn’t settle for a while.
Things have been getting on top of me

I chose “yes, most of the time I haven’t been able to cope at all.” Even little things—like the dishes piling up or the baby having one of those fussy evenings—feel huge. I’ll sit on the couch with her crying in my arms and think, “I can’t do this,” even though I know I somehow get through it every day.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I checked “yes, most of the time.” I lie down exhausted, but my mind starts spinning—did I sterilize the bottles right, is she too hot, too cold, what if I miss something?—and I can’t shut it off. Some nights I’m still awake when she needs her next feeding, and even when I do drift off, any little squeak from the bassinet jerks me awake.
I have felt sad or miserable
I picked “yes, most of the time.” It’s like a heavy blanket I can’t shake off. Even when the baby smiles or someone brings me coffee, the sadness is still right there in the background.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I chose “yes, most of the time.” Pretty much every day this week I’ve ended up in tears—sometimes it’s just a quiet sob in the shower, sometimes it’s full-on crying while I rock her because I feel like I’m failing her.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
I marked “never.” I’ve felt overwhelmed and cried a lot, but I haven’t had any thoughts of hurting myself.

You've shared how the past week has felt heavy-laughing now feels forced, planned outings seem like chores, and guilt creeps in whenever your baby struggles to settle. Daily crying, middle-of-the-night panic, and the constant sense that you're not coping leave you exhausted and discouraged, yet you remain clear that self-harm is not on your mind.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 22, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient explicitly selected the option "yes, some of the time" and described recurrent self-blame when the baby won’t settle, matching that option.</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly chose 'yes, quite a lot' and describes intense, frequent panic episodes with physical symptoms and repetitive checking behaviors.</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly selects the highest-severity option and vividly describes feeling overwhelmed by routine tasks, consistent with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly selected "yes, most of the time" and describes nightly insomnia driven by anxious rumination that persists even after lying down exhausted.</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly chose "yes, most of the time" and described persistent, pervasive sadness that overshadows positive moments.</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS items map onto core criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: anhedonia (Q1-2, scores 1-1), marked guilt (Q3, 2), prominent anxiety and panic without clear triggers (Q4-5, 3-3), subjective inability to cope (Q6, 3), mood-related insomnia (Q7, 3), pervasive sadness (Q8, 3), and frequent crying (Q9, 3). Total of 22 places you well above the 14-point threshold that signals probable depression and urgent referral. Absence of self-harm thoughts (Q10, 0) is reassuring but does not reduce the need for rapid clinical review. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal psychiatrist within the next few days
2. Request evaluation for both <med>postpartum depression</med> and <med>anxiety disorders</med>; discuss medication and therapy options compatible with breastfeeding
3. Plan daily 15-minute support check-ins with partner, family, or friend until professional review
4. Practice 4-7-8 breathing or grounding exercises when <sym>panic sensations</sym> arise; keep baby within safe reach while doing so
5. Lower household expectations-dishes can wait; focus on one small, manageable task per day to reduce feeling overwhelmed
6. Continue voicing thoughts and worries; share this EPDS result openly with your clinician
7. If mood worsens, self-harm thoughts emerge, or panic becomes unbearable, seek emergency care or call perinatal crisis line immediately
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 22: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – EPDS responses reviewed 6 wk PP

Symptom indicators  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, daily tearfulness  
- Marked loss of enjoyment/anticipation for usual activities  
- Excessive guilt/self-blame re infant care  
- Frequent, intrusive “what-if” worry and nocturnal rumination  
- Recurrent panic spells (physical arousal, catastrophic thinking) despite objective infant safety  
- Subjective sense of being overwhelmed “most of the time,” difficulty coping with routine tasks  
- Sleep disturbance driven by anxious rumination, not solely infant demands  

Pattern  
Across-the-board elevation in depressive and anxiety items; no endorsement of self-harm ideation.

Risk factors of screening significance  
1. Depressed mood and anhedonia present ≥ most days  
2. Anxiety symptoms exceed typical postpartum worry (panic-level arousal, repetitive checking)  
3. Functional impairment: sleep loss, task avoidance, perceived inability to cope  
4. Absence of protective factor: inability to access pleasure/humor even when supported  
5. No suicidal ideation endorsed (safety factor)

Screening impression  
Findings are consistent with a high likelihood of major postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; severity indicators (daily crying, “can’t cope,” panic spells) warrant expedited clinical evaluation and possible referral for specialized perinatal mental health assessment.
